pharm: Nilotinib is a selective inhibitor of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia, binding the ATP site of the kinase to block proliferation of BCR-ABL-positive cells. It is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and prolongs the QT interval, the basis of its boxed warning for QT prolongation and sudden death. It must be taken on an empty stomach because food markedly increases absorption and QT-related risk.

summary: Nilotinib (Tasigna) is an oral BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor for Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It carries a BOXED WARNING for QT prolongation and sudden death: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and long QT syndrome must be excluded or corrected before use, and ECGs and electrolytes must be monitored at baseline, 7 days after starting, and periodically and after any dose change. It must be taken on an empty stomach (no food 2 hours before and 1 hour after) because food substantially increases drug exposure and the risk of QT prolongation. It is a CYP3A4 substrate with important interactions, particularly with CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers and other QT-prolonging drugs. Dose is reduced in hepatic impairment.

moa: Nilotinib is an inhibitor of the BCR-ABL kinase, the constitutively active tyrosine kinase created by the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion gene) that drives proliferation of CML cells. It binds with high affinity to the ATP-binding site of BCR-ABL, including many imatinib-resistant mutant forms, inhibiting downstream signaling and inducing apoptosis in BCR-ABL-positive leukemic cells. It also inhibits the receptor tyrosine kinases PDGFR and c-KIT. Nilotinib blocks the hERG potassium channel, which underlies its concentration-dependent QT-interval prolongation. It is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4.

relative: Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Significant baseline cardiac disease or recent myocardial infarction
Total gastrectomy or galactose intolerance/lactase deficiency (capsule contains lactose)
monitor: ECG / QTc at baseline, 7 days after starting, periodically, and after dose changes
Serum potassium and magnesium (keep within normal range)
CBC, liver function tests, lipase, and blood glucose

preg: Nilotinib can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman based on its mechanism and animal data showing embryo-fetal toxicity. Verify pregnancy status before starting. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 14 days after the last dose, and to avoid pregnancy while on therapy.
lact: Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment with nilotinib and for at least 14 days after the final dose. It is unknown whether nilotinib is present in human milk.
renal: No dedicated renal-impairment dose adjustment is specified; nilotinib undergoes minimal renal elimination (excretion is predominantly fecal). Use standard dosing with general caution in significant renal impairment as clinical data are limited.
hepatic: Nilotinib exposure is increased in hepatic impairment and a reduced starting dose is recommended. For newly diagnosed patients with mild, moderate, or severe impairment, start 200 mg twice daily and titrate to 300 mg twice daily as tolerated. For resistant/intolerant patients, mild-to-moderate impairment starts at 300 mg twice daily (titrate to 400 mg BID) and severe impairment starts at 200 mg twice daily (titrate to 300 then 400 mg BID). Monitor LFTs and QTc closely.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit) - increase nilotinib and QT risk; avoid or interrupt/reduce dose
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort) - decrease nilotinib efficacy; avoid
Other QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, methadone, fluoroquinolones) - additive QT prolongation; avoid concomitant use
Drugs that are CYP3A4 substrates with narrow index (e.g., certain statins, ergots, midazolam) - nilotinib may increase their levels
moderate: Acid-reducing agents - separate antacids by >=2 hours; give H2 blockers ~10 h before or 2 h after; PPIs may reduce solubility/exposure
Warfarin and other CYP-metabolized drugs - monitor effect
Drugs affected by P-glycoprotein/BCRP - nilotinib is an inhibitor
minor: Lactose-containing formulation - relevant in galactose intolerance/lactase deficiency
interactions.food: Food substantially increases nilotinib exposure and QT risk - it MUST be taken on an empty stomach (no food 2 h before and 1 h after). Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is established; limit alcohol given additive hepatic and potential cardiac risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause QTc prolongation on ECG, elevated lipase/amylase, elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, hyperglycemia, and electrolyte/blood-count abnormalities.

emergency: Sudden cardiac death or syncope from QT prolongation / torsades de pointes
Acute coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral arterial occlusive event

monitoring: ECG / QTc at baseline, 7 days after initiation, periodically, and after any dose adjustment
Serum potassium and magnesium - correct before starting and keep normal
Complete blood count every 2 weeks for the first 2 months, then monthly
Liver function tests monthly or as clinically indicated
Serum lipase and blood glucose periodically
Cardiovascular status for arterial/venous occlusive events and fluid retention
counsel: Take on an empty stomach - no food for 2 hours before and 1 hour after each dose, twice a day about 12 hours apart
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, which can dangerously raise drug levels
This medicine can affect your heart rhythm - go to the emergency room for fainting, severe dizziness, or palpitations
Keep all appointments for heart tracings (ECG) and blood tests, including potassium and magnesium
Tell your doctor about every other medicine and supplement you take, including St. John's wort and heart-rhythm drugs
Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during and for 14 days after stopping, and should not breastfeed
Report severe abdominal pain, unusual bruising or bleeding, swelling, or signs of infection promptly
pk: Steady state reached in ~8 days of twice-daily dosing
Plasma Tmax ~3 hours after an oral dose
Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C (59-86 F)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: QT prolongation and SUDDEN DEATH - correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia first and monitor ECG at baseline, day 7, and after dose changes
Must be taken on an EMPTY stomach - food sharply increases exposure and QT risk (no food 2 h before, 1 h after)
Avoid concomitant QT-prolonging drugs and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers; avoid grapefruit
Contraindicated in long QT syndrome, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia
Reduce the dose in hepatic impairment and monitor LFTs and lipase
Watch for cardiovascular/arterial occlusive events, pancreatitis, and myelosuppression
missed: If you miss a dose, do NOT take the missed dose or a double dose. Skip it and take your next regular dose at the usual time on an empty stomach. Tell your healthcare provider if you miss doses frequently.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for nilotinib overdose. Overdose may cause myelosuppression, QT prolongation, and other serious effects. Manage with close observation including continuous ECG/cardiac monitoring, correction of electrolyte abnormalities (potassium, magnesium), and supportive care; induce emesis or perform gastric lavage early if appropriate and clinically indicated.
